title: But now (Romans 3:21–26)
hook: the hinge: all have sinned, and all are justified freely by grace

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sin, hamartia, missing the mark. Your line was all of us.

A door weighs far more than its hinge, and the whole door swings on that small piece of metal. Paul's letter to the Romans has a hinge, two words long. For more than two chapters he has built a case like a courtroom closing argument. The nations without the law: guilty. His own people with the law: guilty too. Every mouth stopped, he says. The whole world stands in the dock, and the gavel is about to come down. Then, right where the verdict should be, Paul writes two little words, and the whole letter swings open.
screen: `A DOOR SWINGS ON A HINGE.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD IN THE DOCK.` → `THEN TWO LITTLE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here they are, in the King James Bible: "But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested." But now. In Greek, nuni de. Everything before was the bad news, laid out carefully; everything after is the good news. And Paul doesn't take back a word of the bad news. He says it again: "For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." Nobody is let off. But the very next line is just as wide: "Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus." The same all who fell short are the all who are offered grace. Three words to open. Justified comes from the courtroom: in Greek, being declared in the right, set right with the judge. Freely is the Greek word for a gift, something you don't pay for; John's Gospel uses it when Jesus says they hated him without a cause, for nothing. And grace, charis, is favor you didn't earn. Since the Reformation, Christians have argued about this passage. Protestants in Luther's line hear justified mainly as a verdict: God declares the guilty person righteous, a gift received by faith. Catholics and Orthodox Christians tend to stress that God's grace also makes a person righteous, healing and changing them over a lifetime. Remember the table in Augsburg from day three hundred nine: on the center, Lutherans and Catholics now say they agree. And the hinge is right there in the text. The story doesn't end at all have sinned. It turns on but now.
screen: `NUNI DE: BUT NOW.` · `ALL HAVE SINNED.` · `JUSTIFIED FREELY, AS A GIFT.` · `DECLARED RIGHT, OR MADE RIGHT?` · then, large: `BUT NOW THE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that feels like a final verdict about you: a thing you did, a label you've carried, a sentence that begins I'm the kind of person who. Don't argue with it; on an out-breath, say quietly, but now, and again on the next, not erasing what happened, just letting the story keep going past it. If you pray, hold that verdict before God and leave the next line to God.
But now. Nuni de in Greek. The hinge of Romans, where the verdict of all have sinned swings open into grace.
Your line: the story keeps going. All have sinned is not the last line. Day three hundred fourteen, done.

howItsDone: Christians often learn Romans 3:23–24 by heart; Protestant preaching returns to it again and again, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching reads it alongside baptism and a lifelong healing by grace.

what it means: it's the hinge of Romans. all have sinned, and the same all are offered grace as a gift.
what a scholar hears: dikaioō, to justify, is courtroom language. whether it means declared right, made right, or both is one of the great debates of the Reformation.
